lyric_chord_sync_timeline.acoustic_psychological_mechanism: Deceptive Relative-Minor Shadow (V -> vi): Instead of resolving V -> I, the progression drops into vi (Am), placing the emotional wound ('wreck', 'demons', 'all too well') directly on the minor third (C5 over A1).

lyric_chord_sync_timeline.synchronized_lyric: "Like I'm made of GLASS..." (Demi) | "...less than frickin' PER-fect!" (P!nk) | "This time for AF-ri-ca!" (Shakira)
lyric_chord_sync_timeline.acoustic_psychological_mechanism: Subdominant Horizon Lift & Loop Magnet (vi -> IV -> I): Dropping the bass a third from A to F converts minor grief into warm subdominant yearning that pulls endlessly back to Bar 1.

onomatopoeia_and_prosody_analysis: Why does the human brain fall for the '4 Chords, 23 Songs' comedy illusion? Because I - V - vi - IV is a complete 4-stage psychological narrative arc compressed into 4 bars: Bar 1 (I) states the self ('I'm going under'), Bar 2 (V) reaches outward ('no one to save me'), Bar 3 (vi) suffers the deceptive minor twist ('wreck me / where my demons hide'), and Bar 4 (IV) opens the chest in yearning release ('like I'm made of glass / this time for Africa'). Because IV resolves plagally back to I without closing the drama like a hard V->I period, the loop is an infinite conveyor belt of human emotion.
slm_syntactic_prosody_rule: Four-Chord Pop Trans-Coherence Arc (I -> V -> vi -> IV): Structure 4-part sentences or paragraphs as (1) clear tonic thesis, (2) active outward projection, (3) candid minor-key vulnerability or nuance, and (4) warm, forward-looking synthesis.

onomatopoeia_and_prosody_analysis: In Baroque music, J.S. Bach wrote 'Quodlibets' (Goldberg Variations Var. 30) where multiple popular folk tunes were sung at the exact same time over a ground bass. slm_syntactic_prosody_rule: Three-Voice Pop Quodlibet Synthesis (Country Roads + Edge of Glory + Where Is the Love?): Weave three seemingly disparate examples or domains together simultaneously by aligning them on their shared structural invariant.

lyric_chord_sync_timeline.acoustic_psychological_mechanism: Minor Plagal Self-Collapse (E -> Eb -> D): The major third E wilts to Eb—a SECOND note that does not belong in G Major—at the exact instant Thom Yorke sings 'I don't belong here'. Pitch and semantics become 100% isomorphic.

onomatopoeia_and_prosody_analysis: Radiohead's 'Creep' is the supreme monument of Lyric-to-Harmony Isomorphism in modern rock. While the song is a 4-chord loop (G -> B -> C -> Cm), two of its four chords (B Major with D#, and C Minor with Eb) contain notes that DO NOT BELONG to the key of G Major. Thus, when the singer confesses 'I don't belong here,' the chord itself is a harmonic outcast inside its own key.
slm_syntactic_prosody_rule: Radiohead 'Creep' Chromatic Wire Prosody (I -> III -> IV -> iv / D -> D# -> E -> Eb -> D): Begin in plain reality (I), introduce an unexpected, luminous outsider perspective (III), rise to a high ideal (IV), and resolve with candid, humble self-awareness (iv -> I).

In Radiohead's 'Creep', Jonny Greenwood's three dead-note guitar blasts right after 'I wish I was special' are not decorative rhythm; they are the literal sonic onomatopoeia of a repressed heart snapping under pressure. On the Concert Grand Piano, this translates to three low-register percussive cluster strikes (G1+Ab1+D2+F#2 at 0.98 velocity) punctuated by razor-sharp micro-silences before the three-octave G5->B5 chorus.
slm_syntactic_prosody_rule: Greenwood 'Creep' Psychological-Snap Onomatopoeia Prosody: When describing a sudden realization, emotional turning point, or paradigm fracture, follow a quiet, measured observation with three short, percussive, staccato syllables—then open into full cathartic clarity.
